Spec is the order slip. Status is what is on the table.

The order slip.

What the runtime actually applied.

When they disagree, a resize is in flight.

When pods churn, after other resizes, on a timer.

Deferred is about room, not restarts.

Four states the kubelet tracks.

Desired

Your spec. What the PATCH asked for.

→

Allocated

Admitted. The kubelet intends to apply it.

→

Actuated

Sent to the runtime over CRI.

→

Actual

Live in the cgroup. What status reports.

A Deferred resize is stuck between the first two. The order is on the slip; the line has not fired it yet.

Does Karpenter see a Deferred resize?

Yes
No

No. Karpenter watches the Pending line. A deferred resize is already running.

CPU waits. Memory does not.

CPU is compressible — the worst case is throttling.

Memory is not. The pod can die before room appears. So the pods that might grow memory are the ones that get a PriorityClass.

Node is full? Make room, cheapest step first.

  • Give it a PriorityClass — before the pressure hits
  • Let the kubelet retry — a Deferred resize is not dead
  • Evict the filler — room appears, the resize lands
  • Keep headroom as policy — packed node + growth can't both win

A watchdog you can build today.

resize Deferred
resize landed ✓
60s

A small controller: watch for a resize stuck Deferred past a timeout, then evict the lowest-priority filler. Room frees, the kubelet lands the resize.

1.37 alpha: the scheduler makes room.

scheduler preempts ↓
low priority
high priority — wants to grow

A high-priority resize goes Deferred → the scheduler evicts a lower-priority pod on that same node → the resize completes.

Node-scoped. Respects PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful shutdown. Off by default — alpha.

The escape hatch: recreate, and Karpenter lands it.

Recreate bigger

Pending
→

Karpenter sees Pending

lands here

Give up the live resize, recreate at the bigger size → the new pod is Pending → Karpenter provisions a right-sized node and it lands. The price is the restart.

What your nodes need.

  • cgroup v2 — the documented requirement. EKS AL2023 and GKE COS ship it by default.
  • A recent runtime — containerd 1.6.9+, CRI-O 1.24.2+. EKS AMIs ship containerd 2.x.
  • kubectl 1.32+ — for the --subresource=resize flag.
  • Kubernetes 1.35 for GA — stable on EKS since January 2026.

In production, a machine drives it.

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler watches usage and resizes for you.

One rule: never aim VPA and HPA at the same metric — they chase each other forever.

VPA stopped evicting first.

new recommendation
↓
try /resize in place
↓
done, no restart

if in-place fails, the mode decides

InPlaceOrRecreate

Evict and recreate, like the old days.

InPlace

Never evict. Retry the resize forever.

apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: InPlaceOrRecreate

Needs VPA 1.6+, Kubernetes 1.33+. InPlace is for the pods you cannot restart.

When does VPA actually act?

  • Requests drift outside its recommended range
  • A quick OOM — it reacts fast to out-of-memory
  • A long-running pod, over twelve hours old, more than ten percent off

It learns from eight days of history by default — so a brand-new seasonal spike can still surprise it.

Extra CPU for startup, given back when Ready.

Pending→Running→Ready

Starting: 2x CPU for the first minute.Ready: boost returned, in place. No restart.

# shape per AEP-7862
spec:
  startupBoost:
    cpu:
      type: Factor
      factor: 2
      durationSeconds: 60

Field shape per AEP-7862. Verify against your VPA version.

Slow Java startup? Borrow CPU for a minute. Give it back. Zero restarts.

QoS is frozen at birth.

A resize cannot change it.

Guaranteed stays requests equal limits.

Some pods can't resize at all.

  • Windows pods
  • Non-restartable init containers and ephemeral containers
  • Pods pinned by the static CPU or memory manager policy
  • Swap-memory pods resizing memory without a restart policy

Restartable init containers — the sidecars — can be resized. Know the list before you design around it.

Memory shrink is the risky move.

For JVMs and Node: set memory to RestartContainer.

A planned restart beats a surprise OOM.

Requests can change. They can never be removed.

A stuck resize is silent.
